Series::kthvalue¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::kthvalue(std::int64_t k) const -> Series
Series::kthvalue(std::int64_t k, std::int64_t dim) const -> Series
Series::kthvalue(std::int64_t k, std::int64_t dim, bool keepdim) const -> Series

What It Does¶

kthvalue() selects one order statistic: the k-th smallest value in each chosen lane. It does not return an index, and it does not require materializing a full user-visible sorted result. Its rank is one-based, so k=1 means the smallest value and k=size(dim) means the largest.

The default uses the final axis. dim chooses another axis. keepdim decides whether the reduced axis disappears or survives as length 1; that is useful when the selected value will broadcast back against the original series.

Parameters¶

k (std::int64_t)

The one-based ascending rank. It must satisfy 1 <= k <= size(dim). Duplicate values occupy separate ranks: for [1, 1, 3], rank 1 and rank 2 are both 1.

dim (std::int64_t)

The axis within which ranks are evaluated. Negative dimensions normalize from the end.

keepdim (bool)

  • false: remove dim from the result shape.

  • true: retain it with length 1.

The selected value is unchanged; only result alignment changes.

Returns¶

Series The selected value or values, represented as float64 on the current surface. It does not return the source positions.

Examples¶

Example 1. The third smallest value is the middle ordered value here.

auto scores = pluss::make_series({3.0, 1.0, 4.0, 1.0, 5.0});
std::cout << scores.kthvalue(3);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=3

The ordered values are [1, 1, 3, 4, 5]; k=3 therefore selects 3.

Example 2. The endpoints recover the smallest and largest order statistics.

std::cout << scores.kthvalue(1) << "\n";
std::cout << scores.kthvalue(5);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=1
pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=5

Example 3. dim=0 selects one ranked value per column.

auto table = pluss::make_series({{4.0, 1.0, 3.0}, {2.0, 5.0, 1.0}});
std::cout << table.kthvalue(2, 0);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[2], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=false)
data=[4, 5, 3]

Example 4. keepdim=true preserves the ranked axis for later broadcasting.

std::cout << table.kthvalue(2, 1, true);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,1], strides=[2,2], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=false)
data=[[3],
  [2]]

Example 5. Zero is not a valid rank.

try { std::cout << scores.kthvalue(0); }
catch (const std::exception& error) { std::cout << error.what(); }

Output¶

kthvalue: k must be >= 1

Example 6. A rank beyond the lane length also fails.

try { std::cout << scores.kthvalue(6); }
catch (const std::exception& error) { std::cout << error.what(); }

Output¶

kthvalue: k must be <= size(dim)

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • k is one-based; it is not a zero-based element offset.

  • kthvalue() returns values. Use argsort() or topk_pair() when source positions are required.

  • Complex-valued inputs are rejected because this operation requires ordering.

  • This is an ascending rank. To obtain the r-th largest value in a lane of length n, request k = n - r + 1.

Summary¶

Use kthvalue() when one rank is the answer: thresholds, medians of odd-sized lanes, and rank-based cutoffs. Use topk() or sort() only when several or all ordered values are actually needed.
